rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything
quote: the whole thing from the porch with a coffee
why: 'the whole thing' is one of the two phrases Rule 27 names by name as filler that has stopped functioning as language
suggestion: Her mother watches from the porch with a coffee.

quote: rides it to the end of the road and back, and her knees come up past the handlebars on every stroke
why: the trivial action (riding) and the consequential detail (the bike is now too small) are coordinated with 'and' as equals instead of one being subordinated to the other
suggestion: rides it to the end of the road and back, her knees coming up past the handlebars on every stroke

rule_name: Paragraph Breaks, Keep One Beat in One Paragraph
quote: We'll get you a bigger one.
why: this line and the reply that follows are set as isolated one-line paragraphs cut off from the porch beat they belong to, splitting a continuous moment into artificially separate events (this is Rule 14's own cited violation example, reproduced verbatim)
suggestion: Fold it into the same paragraph as the porch beat: "Her mother watches from the porch with a coffee. 'We'll get you a bigger one.' 'It's fine.'"

quote: she has never done that in her life
why: a bare narrator superlative ('never... in her life'); the style guide lists this exact family as an automatic-fail in narration, permitted only in dialogue
suggestion: She sings in the shower now, badly and at volume, every day of the summer.

quote: like the matter is settled
why: a newly built, writerly comparison appearing in narration rather than a stock/inherited figure or a line spoken by a character
suggestion: "It's one piece of bread," her father says, and goes back to the grill.

quote: like it is being entered into evidence
why: a specific, invented courtroom simile built by the narrator, not an inherited figure and not spoken by Chloe
suggestion: Chloe holds the hot dog up between two fingers, turning it so he can see all of it.

quote: a concession is a concession however it arrives
why: unquoted narration (indirect discourse) built as mirrored, tautological halves ('X is X'), the symmetry construction the style guide cuts on sight in narration
suggestion: Chloe tells him a concession counts no matter how he gets to it.

rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything
quote: That was the whole of it.
why: a reflexive scene-closer variant of the banned 'and that's the whole thing' / 'and that's the end of it' pattern, adding nothing the prior sentence hadn't already said
suggestion: Cut it; end on "In the car, and only in the car."

rule_name: Let Register Escalate With the Moment, Earn Flatness by Contrast
quote: one hand flat on the table, holding onto the edge of it
why: this is the exact gesture Rule 13 names as the manuscript's recycled flat beat, here rendering hard laughter with the identical physical shorthand the rule says gets reused across unrelated emotional registers
suggestion: Her mother ends up on a kitchen chair, wheezing, both hands over her face.

quote: Her mother has not raised her voice and she does not raise it now.
why: mirrored halves in narration, the same claim stated twice in inverted tense, the symmetry construction the style guide cuts on sight
suggestion: Her mother's voice stays level.

quote: and then the stairs, and then the door
why: three escalating, unequal beats are chained with equal-weight 'and then' coordination instead of subordination that would show the sequence causing itself
suggestion: Then there is the thing Chloe has not built at all, before the stairs, then the door.

quote: the thing Chloe has not built at all
why: 'the thing' stands in for whatever Chloe does here as vague emotional shorthand instead of a specific, nameable action
suggestion: Then there is the sound Chloe has not made before, the stairs, the door.

rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything
quote: for a bit after that
why: 'for a bit' is a universal duration marker of exactly the kind Rule 27 names ('for a second' / 'for a while'), telling the reader nothing about the length or nature of the moment
suggestion: Her mother stays in the hall, then goes through to the kitchen.

rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything
quote: she has been for a while
why: 'for a while' is Rule 27's own named example of a crutch duration marker doing no specific work
suggestion: and she is still looking at it when he sets his boots down

quote: her grandfather is thinking about a question
why: Chloe cannot see her grandfather's thoughts; this is the narrator supplying a non-POV character's interiority, the exact fail named in the style guide ('Sam thinks about it longer than he wants to')
suggestion: while her grandfather turns his coffee cup without drinking from it

rule_name: Undercut the Achievement in the Same Breath
quote: which held eleven pounds. That was second in the room.
why: Rule 9 requires the number and the rank that deflates it to share one breath; splitting them into two sentences lets the reader register the eleven pounds as impressive before the rank arrives to undercut it
suggestion: which held eleven pounds, second in the room.

quote: Margie thinks about this for long enough that it is clear nobody has ever asked her before, in Ohio or anywhere else
why: Margie is not the POV character; the narrator reports her thinking and asserts a fact about her entire life history that Chloe has no way of knowing
suggestion: Margie is quiet long enough that the question seems new to her.

quote: Margie thinks about this for long enough
why: states that thinking occurred rather than rendering any texture of it, a summary of cognition standing in for an instance of it
suggestion: Margie's mouth opens, closes, opens again.

quote: Chloe thinks about that for a day and a half
why: nearly identical to the rule's own banned example ('She thought about that one for a while'), reporting that thought happened instead of rendering it happening
suggestion: She turns the teacher's line over for a day and a half, then starts reading in Spanish before dinner.

quote: that is not boring for a single minute of it
why: an absolute superlative claim delivered by the narrator, the family the style guide flags as automatic-fail in narration though fine in dialogue
suggestion: and that holds her attention every time the rope swings

rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything
quote: that one is hard for a while
why: 'for a while' is Rule 27's own named crutch duration marker, doing no work specific to this moment
suggestion: that one takes two weeks to get right

quote: It turns out to be nothing
why: 'nothing' is vague emotional shorthand for how the challenge dissolved, rather than a concrete image of what changed
suggestion: It turns out to take two weeks, then no time at all,

quote: the sheet is the sheet
why: tautological mirrored halves in narration ('X is X'), the symmetry construction the style guide cuts on sight
suggestion: and there is no arguing with the sheet

rule_name: Filtering, Cut "She Sees / Hears / Notices / Knows"
quote: before she sees the oval, but after that she sees it every time she picks it up
why: routes Chloe's recognition of the flaw through the filter verb 'sees' twice instead of rendering the oval itself as the thing she can no longer unsee
suggestion: for three weeks before the oval in the handle catches her eye; after that it's there every time she picks the mallet up

quote: because he has better things to do in November
why: an unearned 'because' clause supplying the teacher's motive as narrator-asserted fact instead of showing it, the obvious-causal-clause fail the style guide cuts
suggestion: She asks again in November and gets it in four words.

rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything
quote: the thing I keep asking you for
why: 'the thing' is the exact placeholder Rule 27 names for behavior that should be shown instead of labeled; what the matching actually requires is never rendered
suggestion: She's doing the breath-drop before the note that I keep asking you for

rule_name: Talking Heads, Anchor Dialogue in Physical Space
quote: Ellie Peterson's out till ten.
why: this opens a six-turn exchange (through line 73) with no physical detail dropped in after the initial framing, so the argument reads as a transcript rather than two bodies in a front hall
suggestion: Add a beat mid-run, e.g. her mother resettling the phone book on the hall table before "Ellie Peterson is ten years old..."

rule_name: The Said-Bookism Overcorrection, Vary Attribution in Long Exchanges
quote: You're not at school. Are you.
why: six consecutive dialogue turns (63-73) carry no attribution at all, so the reader has to track who is speaking purely by counting line breaks and inferring from content
suggestion: "You're not at school," her mother says. "Are you."
